Give each pay rise a job: chart the split between saving and lifestyle spending

Use four graphics to trace repeated take-home increases into extra contributions, extra spending and a long-term savings balance.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a saving rule for repeated net-pay increases

Hypothetical repeated net-pay increase, not a salary or investment forecast. Year one has only the starting monthly saving. At the start of each later year, monthly take-home pay increases by the same entered dollar step; earlier increases continue. The chosen percentage of all accumulated raises adds to monthly saving and the rest is assigned to additional spending. Ordinary spending and the original saving must already fit the starting household budget. Existing savings grow immediately; deposits arrive at month-end. The return is effective annual, converted to an equivalent monthly rate. No account limits, employer match, taxes, fees, job interruption or inflation adjustment are calculated. Dollar increases are nominal: a household must separately budget higher essential costs before treating a raise as available.

The central idea

A repeatable saving rule can make a series of small pay increases meaningful. The larger balance requires real contributions and less spending along the way.

01

Begin with the increase that actually reaches the budget

A raise expressed as a percentage of gross salary does not directly tell you how much more can be spent or saved. Deductions, benefit costs and payroll contributions can change the amount reaching the bank account. Start with an independently checked increase in take-home pay, then decide which new expenses that money must cover.

This example uses a fixed dollar increase in monthly take-home pay at each annual anniversary. Year one has no increase. The first step arrives at the start of year two and continues thereafter. Another equal step begins in year three. This is a hypothetical income path, not a forecast of wages or a promise of annual raises.

FCAC’s budgeting guidance brings income, spending, saving and changing circumstances into the same review. The tool starts after that review: its original monthly saving must already be affordable, and the entered increases must be available after any separately planned rise in essential costs.

02

A small recurring increase accumulates into a larger pool

Suppose the assumed monthly take-home increase is CAD 150 each year. Monthly income in year two is CAD 150 higher than at the start; in year three it is CAD 300 higher. By year ten, nine increases make the monthly difference CAD 1,350. These are accumulated additions to recurring income, not a single annual bonus.

The selected saving share applies to that accumulated pool. With a 50% rule, half of each increase adds to monthly saving and half adds to spending. Earlier saving increases continue when the next increase arrives. The first chart annualizes both parts, so each bar equals twelve times that year’s monthly pool.

The chart excludes original spending and original saving to keep the new-money decision visible. A larger bar later in the period comes from the assumed sequence of increases. It is not evidence that investments generated additional salary or that spending has automatically remained affordable.

03

Compare saving rules with the income path held constant

The three curves share starting savings, original monthly contributions, the pay-rise schedule, the assumed return and the finish date. They differ only in how much of each raise is saved. Saving none of the raises preserves only the original saving habit. Saving all assigns the entire increase to the account. The selected rule sits between those endpoints.

These are different consumption choices. A household on the all-saving path has less additional spending during the period. Calling its larger endpoint better investment performance would confuse effort with return. The same assumed investment return applies to every path.

Try a zero return first. The difference between endpoints then equals the additional cash contributed. Next test a lower or negative return to see how the investment assumption changes the outcome without changing the pay-rise commitment.

04

Separate the saving effort from the investment effect

The waterfall subtracts the zero-capture path from the selected path. Common starting savings and original deposits cancel. The first step is the total extra contributions funded by the rule. The second is the difference between the resulting extra wealth and those contributions: growth when positive, an investment loss when negative.

The monthly return is (1 + annual return)1/12 − 1. Each month, the existing account grows at that rate before the month-end deposit arrives. Every deposit therefore gets only the remaining months of growth; the calculation does not give a late deposit the return earned by the initial balance.

For N whole years and a fixed monthly pay-rise step S, the cumulative extra contributions are 12 × S × saving share × N(N − 1) ÷ 2. This formula checks the saving effort independently of any investment return. All amounts are nominal CAD before account taxes and fees.

05

Choose a rule that survives changing circumstances

The matrix varies the saved percentage and planning horizon. It shows additional ending savings relative to saving none of the raises over the same number of years. A thirty-year case contains more assumed pay increases than a ten-year case, so the gap combines more contributions with more time for investment growth.

A household might first assign part of an observed increase to essentials, then divide what remains between saving and optional spending. That real-world sequence is separate from this simplified tool. Inflation, caregiving, changing hours and a missed raise can all reduce the amount available.

Write the rule in monthly dollars and review it when actual pay changes. An automatic transfer can implement a feasible decision, but it should follow the cash-flow check. Use the multiple-goal guide to decide where the extra saving goes; this article does not choose an account, set contribution room or rank goals for you.
